Illustrated hard surfaces have flat planes, very small bevels that catch a highlight line, and perfectly flat shading per plane.
techniques.how_to_implement_in_python_blender: Generate these parts with bmesh instead of SDF: bmesh.ops.create_cube / create_cone / create_circle, then extrude_face_region, inset_region and bisect_plane, then bm.to_mesh(me). Modifiers: b = ob.modifiers.new('Bevel', 'BEVEL'); b.width = 0.0015-0.003; b.segments = 2-3; b.limit_method = 'ANGLE'; b.angle_limit = radians(30); b.profile = 0.7; b.harden_normals = True; b.miter_outer = 'MITER_ARC'; b.use_clamp_overlap = True; b.face_strength_mode = 'FSTR_AFFECTED'. Then w = ob.modifiers.new('WN', 'WEIGHTED_NORMAL'); w.mode = 'FACE_AREA'; w.weight = 50; w.keep_sharp = True; w.use_face_influence = True. Mark sharp edges with me.set_sharp_from_angle(angle=radians(30)) (4.1+). If a part must stay SDF-generated: bpy.ops.mesh.dissolve_limited(angle_limit=radians(5)), or a DECIMATE modifier with decimate_type = 'DISSOLVE' and angle_limit = radians(3), to recover flat planes, then bevel. Because split normals will break an inverted hull, the outline must use the smoothed _OUTLINE_N attribute from the outline technique. Give the bevel faces a spec/matcap mask of 1 so they read as highlight lines.
techniques.how_to_reproduce_in_threejs: No special code: hardened split normals export as duplicated vertices in glTF, and the toon shader keeps each plane flat. The outline pass must read outlineNormal instead of normal, or the hull will tear at every hard edge. Combine with the banded metal matcap and fwidth specular so bevels produce thin, crisp highlight lines.

techniques.name: Toon-friendly topology: relaxed or remeshed surfaces reprojected onto the SDF, with a sane triangle budget
techniques.problem_it_solves: Raw marching cubes plus collapse decimation produces slivers and fans. Normal interpolation across badly shaped triangles makes the shadow edge zig-zag even with good normals, makes feature-edge and crease detection noisy, and costs a lot: 885k triangles, 609k in the web copy, against roughly 60-150k for a typical game character. That weight also doubles in the outline pass and in any depth pre-pass.
techniques.how_to_implement_in_python_blender: After marching cubes: (1) Relax and reproject. A few Taubin/Laplacian iterations (or a CORRECTIVE_SMOOTH modifier with smooth_type = 'LENGTH_WEIGHTED', use_only_smooth = True, iterations = 5, factor = 0.5), then snap back to the exact surface with 1-2 Newton steps p -= f(p)*grad f(p)/|grad f(p)|^2 using the part's SDF. Triangle shape improves while the surface stays exact. (2) Or remesh: bpy.ops.object.quadriflow_remesh(mode='FACES', target_faces=N, use_mesh_symmetry=True, use_preserve_boundary=True, preserve_attributes=False, seed=0). It needs a manifold mesh and loses data layers, so run it before writing attributes and normals, and reproject afterwards. (3) Budgets: head 10-15k, body 15-25k, coat 15-25k, hair 20-30k, hands about 4k each, props about 10k, for roughly 120k total. Protect silhouette-critical areas (fingers, face contour, hair tips) with the Decimate modifier's vertex_group and vertex_group_factor. (4) Only then compute normals, the outline attribute and the control attributes.
techniques.how_to_reproduce_in_threejs: Nothing new in the shader. Fewer, better-shaped triangles give straighter shadow edges, cheaper outline and depth passes, and smaller files. Keep Draco (raise its quantization as noted in the export technique) or use meshopt via gltfpack, and re-check with the normal debug view.

techniques.name: Procedural hand-painted detail: vertical gradients, darker seams, trim bands, stitches and faint brush noise, as vertex colour or baked texture
techniques.problem_it_solves: Flat single-colour materials read as clay or plastic. Gacha-game textures add subtle hand-painted cues: lighter tops and darker bottoms (BLUE PROTOCOL darkens the lower legs to ground the character), darker colour near seams and edges, contrasting trim bands along hems, stitch dashes, and very low-contrast brush texture. These cues tell the eye that the surface was illustrated.
techniques.how_to_implement_in_python_blender: Compute a geodesic distance to each cloth piece's boundary: G = sparse edge graph weighted by edge lengths; dist, pred, src = scipy.sparse.csgraph.dijkstra(G, indices=boundary_verts, min_only=True, return_predecessors=True). The sources array gives each vertex its nearest boundary vertex, so propagate the boundary arc length s (cumulative length along each boundary loop) as s_v = s[src]. Store '_LINE' (FLOAT2: dist, s). Because the meshes are dense, start with per-vertex colour modulation, which needs no UVs. albedo_mod = gradient (1.04 at the top of each piece falling to 0.94 at the bottom, from object-local z) x seam darkening (1 - 0.12*exp(-dist/0.004)) x noise (1 ± 0.03 from 3D value noise at about 3 cm). Write it to a '_PAINT' FLOAT_COLOR attribute. Trim bands get their own colour where dist < trim_width. When the meshes are reduced, bake to a texture instead: bpy.ops.uv.smart_project(angle_limit=radians(66), island_margin=0.004); build an Emission material from Attribute('_LINE') and Attribute('_PAINT') -> ShaderNodeMapRange / ShaderNodeValToRGB (trim, then a 0.5 mm dark line, then base) plus ShaderNodeTexNoise(scale 25, detail 2) at 3% contrast; create a 2048^2 image node and make it active; set scene.render.engine = 'CYCLES' and scene.cycles.samples = 1; call bpy.ops.object.bake(type='EMIT', margin=8, use_clear=True); save the image and connect it as the glTF Base Color.
techniques.how_to_reproduce_in_threejs: Vertex-colour version: attribute vec4 paint; in the fragment shader litCol *= vPaint.rgb and shadeCol *= vPaint.rgb. The tint/ramp then derives the shade hue from the modulated base, which the current uUseMap path already does for the face. Texture version: generalise uUseMap to every material, with base = texture2D(uMap, vUv).rgb, lit = base, and shade = base*tint from the ramp. Do not bake lines thinner than about 2 texels; draw those with the vertex-distance or inner-line techniques.

techniques.name: Resolution-independent hem, seam and stitch lines from per-vertex distance fields (the GGXrd vertex-data idea)
techniques.problem_it_solves: Lines painted into textures blur or pixelate in close-ups. GGXrd avoided texture detail because vertex data interpolates linearly and does not depend on resolution, and drew inner lines as axis-aligned beams in a texture to keep them free of jaggies. Procedural cloth has no hand-made UVs, so a per-vertex distance field plus fwidth gives the same crisp, zoom-proof lines for hems, trims and stitches with no textures.
techniques.how_to_implement_in_python_blender: Reuse the '_LINE' attribute (geodesic distance to the cloth boundary, plus boundary arc length) from the procedural-detail technique. Interpolated distance is exact for a line on the boundary itself: boundary triangles have d = 0 on the boundary edge, so the iso-lines run parallel to it. For lines offset inward (trim edges, stitch rows 3-6 mm in), make sure at least two triangles span the band, for example by subdividing edges within 1 cm of the boundary with bmesh.ops.subdivide_edges(bm, edges=near, cuts=1, use_grid_fill=True) before computing distances. Also add a 0.5-1 mm rolled hem: the existing SOLIDIFY with use_rim = True gives thickness, and a 1-segment bevel on the rim catches a highlight.
techniques.how_to_reproduce_in_threejs: float d = vLine.x; float aa = fwidth(d); float hem = 1.0 - smoothstep(uHemW - aa, uHemW + aa, d); float trimL = 1.0 - smoothstep(uLW - aa, uLW + aa, abs(d - uTrimOff)); float st = step(0.5, fract(vLine.y*uStitchFreq)) * (1.0 - smoothstep(uSW - aa, uSW + aa, abs(d - uStitchOff))); col = mix(col, uTrimCol*shadeFactor, step(d, uTrimOff)); col = mix(col, uInk, max(max(hem, trimL), st*0.8)). Widths are in metres (about 0.6 mm hem line, about 0.4 mm stitches, stitch frequency about 400 per metre). For constant pixel width, scale them by the view depth.

techniques.name: Designed cloth folds: a few large pipe, zig-zag and tension folds in the SDF, with normals, AO and lines tuned for toon rendering
techniques.problem_it_solves: Offset-surface clothing is perfectly smooth, so it looks like painted skin or clay. Simulated or noise wrinkles create toon blotches instead. Anime clothing uses a few large, designed folds with sharp valleys and rounded ridges: pipe folds hanging from support points (the coat tails), zig-zag folds at elbows and knees, spiral folds on sleeves, tension folds radiating from pull points. The hem silhouette becomes a zig-zag. Valleys carry lines and shadow; ridges stay lit.
techniques.how_to_implement_in_python_blender: Displace the cloth SDF before marching cubes, or move the offset-surface vertices along their normals. Pipe folds on the coat: th = arctan2(y - cy, x - cx); s = clip((z_top - z)/(z_top - z_hem), 0, 1); disp = A*s**1.5*(abs(sin(0.5*n_folds*th + phase)) - 0.6), with A = 4-8 mm and n_folds = 5-9 per panel. The abs(sin) gives V-shaped valleys and rounded ridges, and the amplitude grows toward the hem to produce a zig-zag hem silhouette. Joint folds: for an elbow or knee with axis a and centre c, u = (p - c)·a; disp = A*exp(-u*u/σ²)*tri(k*u + α*sign(p·side)), using a triangle wave and alternating diagonal orientation. Then three adjustments for toon: (1) normals = 0.4*n_geo + 0.6*n of the unfolded surface, so folds read through lines and AO rather than noisy shading; (2) _CTRL.r about 0.2 at concave valley vertices, which gives painted-looking fold shadows; (3) outline width _CTRL.g = 0.1 in valleys (ARC's floating-line fix), and valley edges feed the inner-line extraction.
techniques.how_to_reproduce_in_threejs: Nothing new beyond the control attribute, outline width and inner lines; the folds come from geometry and data. Check that valleys show as thin lines plus a dark sliver rather than as blotches. If blotchy, raise the unfolded-normal weight.

techniques.name: Hair shadow on the face from a screen-space offset of hair-only depth
techniques.problem_it_solves: With shadow maps disabled for clean toon shading, the bangs cast no shadow on the forehead and eyes, so hair looks pasted on. The anime hair shadow is a clean band that follows the hair shape and is offset toward the light. Star Rail approximates it by comparing the face depth with a hair-only depth texture sampled at a light-direction offset.
techniques.how_to_implement_in_python_blender: Static approximation for Blender renders and as a web fallback: for face vertices, cast rays toward the key light with mathutils.bvhtree.BVHTree.FromObject(hair_ob, depsgraph) and hit = bvh.ray_cast(p + n*1e-4, L, 0.05). Where hit is not None, lower _CTRL.r to about 0.2, then blur the values over the vertex graph (normals.diffuse) and threshold for a clean band. Name the hair objects consistently ('Hair*') so the viewer can put them on their own layer.
techniques.how_to_reproduce_in_threejs: Put hair meshes on layer 1 as well. Each frame render a hair-only depth target (WebGLRenderTarget plus DepthTexture, camera.layers.set(1)), then restore the layers. In the face shader, ported from Star Rail GetHairShadow: float d = lin(gl_FragCoord.z); vec2 uv = gl_FragCoord.xy/uRes; vec2 off = normalize(uLightView.xy) * uHairShadowDist * 0.04 / d; float hd = lin(texture2D(uHairDepth, uv + off).x); float hairLit = step(d, hd); lit *= hairLit. Star Rail also scales the offset by FOV and by log10(screen height). Apply only on the face and neck, where the face map G channel is 1.

techniques.name: Final anime 'diffusion' glow and light rig polish
techniques.problem_it_solves: Even a well-shaded model can look like a raw 3D viewport capture. Anime compositing adds a soft diffusion glow over bright areas and a carefully chosen per-character key light. BLUE PROTOCOL applies a diffusion pass at the end; GGXrd gives each character a dedicated light vector instead of a global light. The effect on the model's crispness is small, but it does unify the image.
techniques.how_to_implement_in_python_blender: Compositor: Render Layers Image -> Glare node (glare_type 'FOG_GLOW', threshold 0.85, mix about -0.7) or a Blur (size 20-40 px) blended with Screen at 15-25% -> Composite. Keep view_transform = 'Standard' (already set; AgX or Filmic would desaturate the toon colours). Use the same view-space key light vector as the viewer, as in the shadow-edge technique.
techniques.how_to_reproduce_in_threejs: EffectComposer with RenderPass plus UnrealBloomPass(new THREE.Vector2(w,h), 0.25, 0.6, 0.85), or a custom pass: out = screen(src, blur(src)*0.2). Then OutputPass, which applies sRGB conversion. Keep the light in view space (LIGHT_VIEW) and expose a per-character preset.
